patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014); Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019); Scranton (USA) → Ciudad del Este (Paraguay): Fr Carlos Urrutigoity; Tehuacán → Los Angeles → Mexico: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera; Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth; Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson; Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role: Lobbying against reform and bankruptcy filings
patterns.role_note: At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims; Catholic, insurance and Scouts lobbying against limitation reform is documented in several states.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role: First inquiry before 2005
patterns.role_note: 2002: USCCB National Review Board / John Jay College study, report Feb 2004. 10,667 allegations; 4,392 clergy accused (about 4% of 109,694 clergy)
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role: Where the children were
patterns.role_note: Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington: Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, still open
patterns.role_note: 3,137 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role: Dictatorship, occupation or war
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved). United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978. Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation. United States — 'Baby Scoop Era' adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies (1945–1973).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2003: PROTECT Act (30 April 2003): US citizens/residents prosecutable for illicit sexual conduct abroad with under-18s whether or not they intended it before travel; maximum raised to 30 years. ICE "Operation Predator" (2003) led to over 11,000 arrests incl. more than 1,100 outside the US 2016: International Megan's Law signed 8 Feb 2016; from 31 Oct 2017 passports of covered offenders carry a unique identifier; 21-day advance notice of foreign travel; Angel Watch notifies destination countries
patterns.pattern_summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days (police ran abuse sites to catch users). Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 49,021 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (16% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role: 5 or more cases
patterns.role_note: United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978; United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions; Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation; Los Angeles County juvenile halls and MacLaren Children's Center — $4bn settlement; New Hampshire Youth Development Center, Manchester; US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018; Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'; Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge; Epstein — 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 state plea; Epstein — 2019 federal sex-trafficking indictment and death in custody; Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor; Zorro Ranch, New Mexico — state probe dropped in 2019, reopened 2026; Epstein Files Transparency.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Investigations have been state-level (attorneys general, grand juries) and church-commissioned
patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role: Claim investigated and disproved
patterns.role_note: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska. 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria. McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals.
patterns.pattern_summary: Invented trafficking stories take resources from real ones. In July 2020 the US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about a false claim that the furniture seller Wayfair was selling children; the hotline's operator, Polaris, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed it, and none of the reports had new information. "Pizzagate" led to a man firing a rifle inside a Washington restaurant in 2016. London's Metropolitan Police spent over £2 million on Operation Midland, built on a "VIP ring" story invented by Carl Beech, who was himself jailed for child-abuse offences. The McMartin preschool trials in the 1980s cost about $15 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
cases.who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cases.what: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
cases.cover_up: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

cases.title: Pennsylvania grand jury — six dioceses
cases.who: Six Pennsylvania Catholic dioceses
cases.what: A 23-member statewide grand jury report released by Attorney General Josh Shapiro on 14 August 2018 identified 301 'predator priests' and at least 1,000 child victims over about 70 years in six dioceses. The roughly 1,400-page report found bishops 'went to great lengths to keep it secret' and moved abusers. Most crimes were too old to prosecute.
cases.cover_up: Abusers moved and protected, some later promoted; reports brushed aside; most crimes beyond statute of limitations

cases.title: US diocesan bankruptcies and settlements
cases.who: US Catholic dioceses (Portland, Tucson, Spokane, San Diego, Davenport, Milwaukee, Albany and others)
cases.what: Starting with Portland in 2004, at least 13 US dioceses filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy by 2023 under abuse claims. US dioceses have paid about $4 billion to roughly 17,000 victims since the 1980s. In Milwaukee, which filed in 2011 after paying $29 million on about 200 cases, released documents showed abusive priests were moved between assignments without notifying law enforcement.
cases.cover_up: Milwaukee: Cardinal Timothy Dolan, with Vatican approval, moved $57 million into a cemetery trust, which kept it from victims; released files showed priests moved without telling police

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: R. Kelly — racketeering and child sexual abuse material convictions
cases.who: Robert Kelly (singer) and his entourage (racketeering enterprise)
cases.what: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Kelly on 27 Sept 2021 of racketeering, including acts of bribery and sexual exploitation of a child, and of Mann Act sex-trafficking offences; he was sentenced to 30 years. In September 2022 a Chicago federal jury convicted him of three counts of producing child sexual abuse material and three of enticing a minor; in February 2023 he was sentenced to 20 years, 19 of them to run concurrently with the New York term. The 2019 documentary 'Surviving R. Kelly' led to the new prosecutions.
cases.cover_up: He was acquitted in 2008 of child pornography charges brought in 2002, despite Chicago Sun-Times reporting from 2000.

cases.title: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
cases.who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
cases.what: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.
cases.cover_up: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.

cases.title: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
cases.who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
cases.what: The Ideal Maternity Home in Nova Scotia, run by William and Lila Young from the late 1920s until 1947, promised discreet birthing and adoption for unmarried mothers. According to author Bette Cahill, people paid up to $10,000, usually disguised as a donation, to adopt babies from the home, while babies considered 'unmarketable' were fed only molasses and water; many died and were buried in butter boxes. Wikipedia, citing Cahill, adds that mothers were charged $500, that the provincial Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934, and that the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act; a 1946 Montreal Standard article described their 'baby farm rackets'.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
cases.who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
cases.what: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II appointed Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a letter from Cardinal John O'Connor dated 28 October 1999 warning that the appointment would risk serious scandal, and after McCarrick denied the allegations. Benedict XVI did not order an investigation but had McCarrick told to retire in 2006 and keep a lower profile, which he did not do. The report said Francis did not learn that McCarrick was accused of abusing a minor until 2017. On 11 January 2019 the CDF found him guilty of solicitation in confession and sexual offences with minors and adults, and he was dismissed from the priesthood (announced 16 February 2019). A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old at a 1974 wedding reception was dismissed on 30 August 2023 after he was found incompetent to stand trial because of dementia. He died in April 2025.
cases.cover_up: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000

cases.title: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul — Indian priest extradited to Minnesota
cases.who: Diocese of Crookston, Minnesota; diocese in India
cases.what: An Indian priest serving in the Diocese of Crookston in 2004–2005 was removed from ministry in September 2005 and returned to India. He was charged in 2006 with raping a girl from age 14; extradition took about five years after an Interpol alert, with arrest in Erode, India in 2012 and return to Minnesota in November 2014. In 2015 he pleaded guilty to criminal sexual misconduct involving a teenage girl and was sentenced to a year and a day (time served); the rape charges were dismissed under the plea deal and he faced deportation to India.
cases.cover_up: The Vatican recommended his removal from the priesthood, but the Indian bishop instead imposed a year in a monastery through a canonical trial, and he continued as a priest in India.

cases.title: Diocese of Lafayette — Gilbert Gauthe (first national case)
cases.who: Diocese of Lafayette; Fr Gilbert Gauthe
cases.what: Fr Gilbert Gauthe admitted abusing 37 children while serving in the Diocese of Lafayette from 1972 to 1983. In 1974 the bishop made him a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations about altar boys. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years; the diocese paid more than $20 million. His 1984–85 case was the first widely publicised clergy abuse prosecution in the US.
cases.cover_up: Bishop assigned him as Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy in 1976 and returned

cases.title: Epstein — 2019 federal sex-trafficking indictment and death in custody
cases.who: Jeffrey Epstein; Metropolitan Correctional Center (Bureau of Prisons)
cases.what: Epstein was arrested at Teterboro Airport on 6 July 2019 and indicted in Manhattan for sex trafficking of minors in 2002–2005. Bail was denied on 18 July. He died in his cell on 10 August 2019; the medical examiner ruled suicide by hanging and the case was dismissed on 29 August 2019. The DOJ Inspector General's June 2023 report found no evidence contradicting suicide but documented staff failures that made it possible.
cases.cover_up: DOJ Inspector General (June 2023) found negligence and misconduct by Bureau of Prisons staff: 13 employees showed misconduct, two were criminally charged, guards skipped required checks and falsified records, and Epstein was left without a cellmate after an apparent July 23 suicide attempt.

cases.title: Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor
cases.who: Ghislaine Maxwell
cases.what: Maxwell was arrested on 2 July 2020 in Bradford, New Hampshire. On 29 December 2021 a jury convicted her on five of six counts, including sex trafficking of a minor; she was acquitted of enticing a minor to travel. She was sentenced on 28 June 2022 to 20 years. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction on 17 Sept 2024 and the US Supreme Court declined her appeal on 6 Oct 2025; she had argued Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement shielded co-conspirators. As of mid-2026 her lawyer said he would seek a pardon; Blanche said in May 2026 he would not recommend one.
cases.cover_up: In July 2025 Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche interviewed Maxwell with limited immunity; on 1 Aug 2025 she was moved to the minimum-security Federal Prison Camp Bryan, Texas. A DOJ official recorded secretly said the transfer was against policy (DOJ said he had no role).

Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Where children are abused for paying viewers
patterns.role_note: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role: 2 to 4 cases

patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Bishops apologised 9 July 2002; said about 200 of 7,000 priests had sexual misconduct over two decades; at least 34 priests suspended in 2003
patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

cases.title: David Timothy Deakin — life sentence, Angeles City court (2020)
cases.who: David Timothy Deakin (US national)
cases.what: Acting on an FBI referral, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation arrested US national David Timothy Deakin in Mabalacat, Pampanga, in 2017, rescuing two girls and seizing hard drives of abuse material; IJM said he abused Filipino children, recorded it and sold it online to foreign customers. In May 2020 the Angeles City Regional Trial Court Branch 58 convicted him of large-scale human trafficking and sentenced him to life imprisonment, in the country's first conviction delivered by videoconference. The 2025 US TIP report names Angeles City among tourist destinations with high demand for commercial sex.

cases.title: Philippines — foreign offenders and child sex trafficking in tourist towns (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign offenders; family members; brothel and bar operators
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says sex trafficking frequently occurs in tourist destinations such as Boracay, Angeles City, Olongapo, Puerto Galera and Surigao. Many foreign offenders are convicted or charged sex offenders at home, most commonly from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the UK and the US, with more reports from Canada, Morocco, Iraq and Denmark. Courts convicted 143 traffickers, 120 for sex trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity remained significant concerns.

cases.title: Melbourne flight attendant jailed for abusing 26 girls in the Philippines
cases.who: Australian travelling offender (airline flight attendant)
cases.what: On 30 March 2020 a 52-year-old Melbourne flight attendant was sentenced in Australia to 18.5 years' imprisonment (14 years non-parole) for sexually abusing 26 girls aged 12 to 17 in the Philippines on 25 occasions between 2010 and 2017. He was prosecuted in Australia under Commonwealth laws covering child sexual offences committed overseas.

cases.title: Sydney man sentenced after rescue of three children in the Philippines
cases.who: Australian offender abusing children in the Philippines
cases.what: A 64-year-old Sydney man was sentenced on 3 December 2021 to eight years and 10 months for sexual activity with children under 16 outside Australia and producing child abuse material overseas, among other charges. The AFP investigation led to three children being removed from harm in the Philippines in May 2020.

cases.title: Sydney man jailed for persistent abuse of a child in the Philippines
cases.who: Australian offender procuring a child in the Philippines
cases.what: On 17 December 2021 a Sydney man was sentenced to nine years and one month for procuring a child to engage in sexual activity outside Australia and persistent sexual abuse of a child outside Australia, plus abuse-material offences. One child was rescued in the Philippines.

cases.title: Brisbane man jailed for abusing children in the Visayas, Philippines
cases.who: Australian offender abusing children in the Philippines
cases.what: A 57-year-old Brisbane man was sentenced on 31 January 2022 to eight years' imprisonment (four non-parole) for abusing children overseas. Five children were rescued in the Visayas region of the Philippines in December 2019 as a result of the investigation.

cases.title: Philippines blacklists Australian sex offender after AFP warning (2013)
cases.who: Philippine Bureau of Immigration; Australian Federal Police
cases.what: In April 2013 Philippine immigration officers at Manila airport intercepted and blacklisted an Australian convicted in Perth in 2010 of indecent assault on children, travelling on a New Zealand passport and planning to stay in Iloilo, after an Australian police warning that he posed a risk to Filipino children. It is an example of offender travel notifications between countries.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Scale of Harm — prevalence of livestreamed abuse in the Philippines (IJM / Rights Lab)
cases.who: Family members and neighbours paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse
cases.what: IJM and the University of Nottingham Rights Lab estimated the prevalence of trafficking to produce child sexual exploitation material in the Philippines. IJM states that 1 in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022, that the median victim age in its earlier 2020 study was 11, average abuse lasted two years, and 9% of victims were 3 or younger. IJM UK says the UK is among the top three consumer countries.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

cases.title: AUSTRAC v Westpac — payments linked to child exploitation in the Philippines
cases.who: Westpac Banking Corporation (failure to monitor transfers)
cases.what: In November 2019 AUSTRAC alleged Westpac had breached anti-money-laundering law more than 23 million times, including failing to report international funds transfer instructions worth more than A$11 billion; the breaches included failures over suspicious transactions associated with possible child exploitation. The scandal forced the resignation of chief executive Brian Hartzer. On 24 September 2020 Westpac and AUSTRAC agreed a record A$1.3 billion penalty, the largest in Australian corporate history.

cases.title: Australian man directed abuse of two children in the Philippines over Skype
cases.who: Australian offender paying the children's mother
cases.what: In 2016 Task Force Argos executed a warrant at a 58-year-old Australian man's home. Using Skype he conducted 'live remote' sexual abuse of two children in the Philippines, aged two and seven when it began, while paying their mother; it continued for nearly five years. He pleaded guilty to charges including having sex with a child under 16 outside Australia.

cases.title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
cases.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
cases.what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Chile → Peru: Marist Brother Abel Pérez; Germany → South America: Jesuit Fr Wolfgang S..
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status

Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role: First inquiry 2015 on
patterns.role_note: 2018: Vatican investigation (Scicluna and Bertomeu), Feb 2018. Pope Francis admitted "serious mistakes"; all Chilean bishops offered resignation (May 2018); Chile removed limitation period for child sex abuse 11 July 2019
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role: Where the children were
patterns.role_note: Paul Schäfer / Colonia Dignidad: Hopp living in Germany; investigation dropped
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role: Dictatorship, occupation or war
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site (proven link to a state service). Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

cases.title: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
cases.who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
cases.what: The Vatican found Fr Fernando Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011 and sentenced him to a life of prayer and penance; Pope Francis dismissed him from the priesthood on 27 September 2018, announced the next day. Four of his protégés became bishops, including Juan Barros of Osorno, whom Francis had defended. After receiving a 2,300-page report from Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken in his assessment of the situation in Chile. Every bishop in Chile offered to resign in May 2018; by the end of June five resignations, including Barros's (11 June), had been accepted. In October 2018 an appeals court found the Archdiocese of Santiago liable for covering up for Karadima in a suit by three survivors naming Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati.
cases.cover_up: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015

cases.title: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cases.what: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.
cases.cover_up: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.

cases.title: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
cases.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cases.what: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
cases.cover_up: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
cases.who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
cases.what: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.

cases.title: Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes)
cases.who: SENAME-accredited residential care homes (hogares), run by private organisations under state supervision
cases.what: Family-court judges led by Judge Mónica Jeldres, with UNICEF, interviewed children in residential homes between July and November 2012. The report found sexual abuse was a constant in the homes and that 10% of children in state protection had been involved in some form of sexual abuse as victim or perpetrator. In one Arica home it found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers: 24 girls left the home and returned drugged at dawn. After publication the government ordered 34 homes intervened, SENAME closed four residences, the prosecutor's office opened investigations and deputies announced a congressional investigating commission.
cases.cover_up: The report was delivered to the Judiciary in March 2013 but held back over methodological criticism until CIPER published it in July 2013; legislators said the Justice Minister had known since March.

cases.title: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
cases.who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
cases.what: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Romanian man jailed for sextortion linked to a Northern Ireland teenager's suicide
cases.who: Individual offender posing as a girl online
cases.what: A 17-year-old from Coalisland took his own life in June 2015 after a man posing as a girl tricked him into sharing intimate images and blackmailed him. After a joint PSNI–Romanian Police investigation supported by Europol and the NCA, a 31-year-old Romanian was sentenced in Timișoara in 2017 to four years for blackmail and producing and distributing indecent images of a child.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
cases.who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
cases.what: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war, taking children is often a tactic. The International Criminal Court convicted the LRA commander Dominic Ongwen on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role: 5 or more cases
patterns.role_note: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations; MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport; MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations; MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021); Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

cases.title: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
cases.who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
cases.what: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.

cases.title: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
cases.who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
cases.what: An internal UN document revealed by The Guardian in April 2015 recorded interviews with six boys aged 9 to 13 who said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport, in exchange for food rations. The Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014; the investigation eventually covered accusations by fifteen children, most interviewed in Bangui in 2015 and 2016. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case (non-lieu) for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony; the prosecutor said 'it cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged.
cases.cover_up: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.

cases.title: MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021)
cases.who: Gabonese military contingent, MINUSCA
cases.what: On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA (about 450 personnel) would be repatriated after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse; Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most multiple-victim MINUSCA allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.

cases.title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

cases.title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024)
cases.who: CPC coalition (UPC, 3R, anti-balaka); national defence forces; Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe; RSF
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in CAR in 2024: CPC armed groups 58, government and pro-government forces 35 (national defence forces 21, Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe 9), PRNC 11, Sudanese RSF 2. It verified the abduction of 141 children, most for recruitment and/or sexual violence. The Secretary-General said he was deeply concerned by rising violations by government and pro-government forces.

cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.

cases.title: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
cases.who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
cases.what: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained trying to take 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic without proper documentation; their interpreters said group members had spoken with the children's parents. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association. In February a judge released eight, concluding they had not knowingly committed a crime, and later a ninth; the kidnapping and criminal association charges were dropped. On 17 May 2010 the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel under a 1980 law restricting movement out of Haiti and sentenced to the 3 months and 8 days she had already served.

cases.title: Haiti — 2007: children trafficked for international adoption returned to parents
cases.who: A Haitian centre holding children awaiting international adoption
cases.what: In 2007 a Haitian centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting international adoption to their families, after misleading parents with payments and holding the children in 'inhumane conditions' for months or years, according to the International Organization for Migration. An October 2007 report said officials had returned 50 trafficked children with 100 more awaiting rescue.

cases.title: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued
cases.who: Oxfam GB staff in the 2010 earthquake response, including the country director
cases.what: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. The Charity Commission's June 2019 inquiry found that not all lines of enquiry about minors were pursued and that Oxfam did not adequately investigate allegations in an email of 18 July 2011 that minors were being sexually abused by Oxfam employees, nor report them to the Commission or law enforcement. The Commission said it was no longer possible to conclude with certainty whether minors were involved or at risk.
cases.cover_up: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.

cases.title: Haiti — armed gangs' sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024)
cases.who: Viv Ansanm gang coalition (411 cases) and other armed gangs
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children (523 girls, 43 boys) in Haiti in 2024, 411 attributed to the Viv Ansanm coalition; cases involved rape (406) and gang rape (160). This was up from 41 girls verified in 2023. Viv Ansanm was listed in the Secretary-General's annex for rape and other sexual violence against children, recruitment, killing and maiming, and attacks on schools and hospitals.

cases.title: Haiti — restavek child domestic servitude and gang exploitation of children (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Host families (restavek); armed gangs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says a large share of Haiti's trafficking cases involve children in restavek domestic servitude, often physically abused and unpaid, and that displacement from Port-au-Prince increased children's risk of sexual exploitation in the restavek system. Gangs exploit women and girls in sex trafficking; an international organization reported close to 50 per cent of gang members are children, with a 70 per cent rise in child recruitment in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Observers report police and immigration officials complicit at the Haiti–Dominican Republic border.

cases.title: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
cases.who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
cases.what: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.

cases.title: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
cases.who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
cases.what: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.
cases.cover_up: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.

cases.title: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
cases.who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
cases.what: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.
cases.cover_up: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.

cases.title: Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network
cases.who: Brothel and trafficking ring in Tucumán province
cases.what: Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, provoking national protests and calls to impeach the judges. In December 2013 Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of the 13 guilty. Her mother's foundation, created in 2008, says it has helped free hundreds of women and girls from brothels. (Verón was an adult; the case is included because it exposed the national network that also trafficked minors.)
cases.cover_up: Campaigners and the victim's family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect prostitution rings; trial court acquitted all 13 in 2012.

cases.title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)

cases.title: Thorbjørn Jagland — charged with aggravated corruption over Epstein ties

cases.what: After the US Justice Department's 2026 release of Epstein documents, Norway's economic-crime agency Økokrim opened an investigation into former prime minister and Council of Europe secretary-general Thorbjørn Jagland on suspicion of aggravated corruption, looking into 'whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position'. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
cases.who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)

cases.title: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
cases.who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
cases.who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
cases.what: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria; thousands remain missing.

cases.title: Lebanon — Chez Maurice and Silver-B: about 75 Syrian women freed from sex-trafficking ring (2016)

HRW said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk and that the same premises had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found, and later reopened. Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims in 2016, mainly these survivors.
cases.cover_up: Chez Maurice was raided in late 2011 when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found trapped there, closed for about three months and reopened. A survivor told Legal Agenda a trafficker claimed he had 'bought the state'.
