cases.title: AP investigation — sexual abuse in Pakistan's madrassas
cases.who: Islamic seminaries (madrassas), over 22,000 registered with at least 2 million pupils
cases.what: An AP investigation published 21 November 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics was pervasive in Pakistan's madrassas and seldom prosecuted. In one case a 9-year-old's teacher confessed but was freed after the mother 'forgave' him for $300. A follow-up AP investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the same pattern.
cases.cover_up: Police are often paid off and refuse to register cases; families of poor victims are pressured to 'forgive' clerics and accept money, which Pakistani law allows; the religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted.

cases.title: Kasur child abuse video scandal (Hussain Khanwala)
cases.who: Local gang filming abuse of children; Punjab police; local MPA (alleged)
cases.what: In August 2015 it emerged that in Hussain Khanwala village, Kasur district, a gang had filmed the sexual abuse of at least 280 children and blackmailed their parents by threatening to leak the videos. Police, who had failed to act despite pleas from parents, made dozens of arrests only after clashes between relatives and authorities drew media attention. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court in Lahore sentenced two men to life imprisonment; Arab News reported in February 2018 that 12 other accused men were acquitted. Placed in 'elite' for the alleged political protection; the protection claims were not verified for this record.
cases.cover_up: Punjab police and the local PML-N provincial assembly member Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan were alleged to have tried to cover it up; the Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. Police clashed with protesting villagers on 8 Aug 2015.

cases.who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries

cases.title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.
